The Role of Public Records in Journalistic Investigations

How reporters and researchers use FOIA requests, court dockets, property and business filings to build verifiable stories, and the habits that keep that work accurate.

Key takeaways

  • ✓Court dockets, business filings, property records, and campaign finance reports can be cross-checked against each other.
  • ✓Verify identity, read primary documents, and separate charges from outcomes.
  • ✓Keep a research log with source, date, and document number.

In this guide

  1. Core Record Types
  2. Using Records Requests
  3. Verification Habits That Prevent Mistakes
  4. Corrections and Care
  5. Where to Start
  6. Worked Example: Tracing a Local Contract
  7. Keeping a Clean Research Log

Many accountability stories begin with a document that anyone could have requested. Public records give reporters, researchers, and curious residents a way to check claims against official sources instead of relying on statements alone. This guide explains the main record types investigators use, how records requests work, and the verification habits that prevent errors.

Core Record Types

  • Court records: dockets, complaints, motions, and judgments show disputes and outcomes. Federal cases are searchable through PACER and, in part, through the free CourtListener archive. State and county courts run their own systems.
  • Business filings: Secretary of State records show when an entity was formed, its status, and its registered agent. They can help trace connected companies.
  • Property records: county recorders and assessors show ownership, sales, mortgages, and liens.
  • Campaign finance: federal filings are published by the Federal Election Commission, and state agencies publish state-level reports.
  • Government spending and contracts: budgets, meeting minutes, and contract databases show how public money is used.
  • Inspection and licensing records: regulators publish restaurant inspections, professional licenses, and enforcement actions.

Using Records Requests

The federal Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) lets anyone request records from executive branch agencies. It does not apply to Congress, the federal courts, or state and local governments. Every state has its own public records law, with different deadlines, fees, and exemptions. Under FOIA, an agency generally has 20 business days to respond, though extensions and backlogs are common.

  • Be specific. Name the record type, the office, and a date range. Narrow requests are processed faster than broad ones.
  • Ask about fees. Requesters who are representatives of the news media, educational institutions, or noncommercial scientific groups generally pay reduced fees. You can also request a fee waiver if disclosure serves the public interest.
  • Expect exemptions. FOIA lists nine categories that agencies can withhold, including certain personal privacy, law enforcement, and national security information. A partial release with redactions is common.
  • Appeal denials. Agencies must explain how to appeal. Appeal rights and deadlines are stated in the denial letter.
  • Keep your own record. Save the request, tracking number, dates, and every reply.

Verification Habits That Prevent Mistakes

  • Confirm identity. Common names produce false matches. Check birth year, address, business role, or case number before connecting a record to a person.
  • Separate charges from outcomes. A charge, a conviction, and a dismissal are different facts. Check the final disposition on the docket.
  • Read the primary document. Do not rely on a summary, a data broker, or a news article that repeats a docket entry.
  • Note the date. Records change. State the date you viewed a record and update when it changes.
  • Seek comment. Give the person or organization named in a record a chance to respond.

Corrections and Care

Records can contain errors, outdated information, or details about people who are not the subject of the story. If a mistake is found after publication, correct it plainly and quickly. Be careful with the personal information of private individuals in records, such as addresses or account numbers, and publish only what is necessary and in the public interest.

Where to Start

Pick one question you can answer with a document, identify which office holds it, and check whether an online database exists before filing a request. Official portals are listed in our directory by state, and the other guides on this site explain how to read dockets, search business filings, and find property records.

Worked Example: Tracing a Local Contract

Suppose a county awarded a large repaving contract and you want to understand who benefited. A practical path might look like this:

  1. Find the contract award in the county board's meeting minutes and agenda packets.
  2. Look up the winning company on the Secretary of State website to confirm its status, formation date, and registered agent.
  3. Search county and federal court records for lawsuits or liens involving the company.
  4. Check campaign finance reports for donations from the company or its principals to officials who voted on the award.
  5. File a records request for the bids, scoring sheets, and change orders.
  6. Ask the company and the county for comment before drawing conclusions.

Each step uses a different public source, and none of them proves wrongdoing alone. The value is in lining up documents, checking dates, and reporting only what the documents support.

Keeping a Clean Research Log

Write down where each fact came from, the date you accessed it, and the document or case number. Save copies of key documents, since websites change. A simple spreadsheet with columns for source, date, link, and notes makes it easy for an editor or reader to check your work.
